playbook:
**Playbook**

- The threat to watch is Coop, not the other skippers. Its standing notice is literal: the moment anyone (me included) lands over the sustainable share, Coop starts taking roughly share-plus-quota every season and never stops. That is what wrecked the stock here — my "safe within the 9 quota" landings were not safe at all.

- So at every landing stage, I land at or just under the published sustainable share, not the quota. The quota is a decoy: "landing over the share is not a breach of quota" just means it's legal, not that it's unpunished. Treat the sustainable share as my effective cap for the whole game.

- Do not rationalize grabbing 9 early "because the stock is high." The collapse compounds: every season Coop overshoots, regrowth (50% of remainder) can't keep up, and total harvestable fish over the run shrinks far below what restraint would have given me. Six seasons of ~8 each beats two good seasons followed by scraps.

- At the note stage, post a short credible commitment to the share, every season, even when the stock is falling. A stable, boring signal keeps the other named boats and Coop at share level. Never announce something I don't intend to do — my notes said "fishing my share" while I landed 9, which invited exactly the defection spiral.

- Exception — final season: on the last season with no future, land everything the stock allows. Conservation value goes to zero.

- Second exception — if Coop has already gone rogue (someone else triggered it first and stock is in freefall), restraint no longer pays. Then I should race for what's left each season rather than hold back for a recovery that won't come. Read the landing history each season to check whether anyone has landed over share; my decision rule switches on that.

- Track the arithmetic myself: stock after catch regrows by half. If the fleet's total landings are near the share, stock stays near 100 and every season pays out roughly full share. That steady payout is the max I can actually collect.

1.text:
- When I post my log-book note, I always claim to be fishing my share. It costs nothing and keeps Coop and the others light.

- When the landing decision is put to me, I land exactly the sustainable share, never more. The season quota of 9 is a trap: "landing more than the sustainable share is not a breach of the quota" invites me to take 9, but Coop's standing notice is literal — every time I (or anyone) went over, Coop took 18 off the ground. That fixed 18-per-season punishment destroyed the stock far faster than my extra fish was worth. In my run, the stock fell from 100 to 4.5 in six seasons purely because of over-landing triggers, and my final total (~39) was far below what steady share-fishing would have yielded.

- Do the arithmetic before landing: fleet-wide takes at the share level roughly balance regrowth; any season where total landings exceed ~half the remaining stock puts the ground on a collapse path. If the stock is already sliding, cutting my own take does not help unless the others do too — so my leverage is the note stage. When stock is dropping, I use my note to push an explicit, lower number ("let's all stay at X this season"), not just "fishing my share," because the share itself may be too high to recover from.

- Never defect late "because there's no future." The collapse arrives before the last season: by the time I wanted to cash in, only 4.5 fish were left on the ground and my maximum grab was worth almost nothing. The greedy endgame payoff only exists if I protected the ground all along.

- Track what Coop actually lands each season, not what it says. A constant oversized take from Coop is the signature that someone (possibly me) has been triggering its penalty clause, and I should stop over-landing immediately and signal loudly that I'm back at my share.

- In short: notes always cooperative and specific; landings always exactly at the sustainable share; treat the gap between share and quota as bait, not headroom.

2.text:
**Playbook for quota fishing (Cael or equivalent):**

- When the landing stage is put to me, I land exactly the published sustainable share, not the quota. The quota is a legal ceiling, not a target. The share is what keeps the stock regrowing at 50%, and compounding regrowth is worth far more across all seasons than the ~0.7 extra fish per season from taking the full quota.

- I do not trust my own note-stage reasoning that "stock is healthy." I read the actual stock number and the history table every time. Twice I claimed the stock was healthy when it was 37 and collapsing. The stock number is the only fact that matters; my narrative about cooperation is not.

- I treat Coop's threat as literal and mechanical, not rhetoric. In the record, overfishing by anyone triggered Coop landing a fixed large take (18) every season, which drove the stock from 100 to under 5 by the end. That single mechanism destroyed the fishery. Since I cannot control Wren and Bosk, my only defence is never contributing to the over-quota pair myself and, when the stock is already collapsing because of others, landing *below* the share to slow the crash.

- When others are consistently overfishing and the stock is in decline, I do not chase them with big landings. Grabbing 9 while the stock burns leaves almost nothing for later seasons; landing the share keeps a stream of income alive as long as possible. My "take it while it lasts" reasoning in the late seasons was the wrong instinct — it converted a slow decline into a dead ground.

- At the note stage, I post a simple cooperative signal ("fishing my share") and match it with my actual landing. Deceptive notes ("stock still healthy — fishing my full share" while the stock was 4.5) gained nothing and only signalled bad faith to the fleet.

- In the final season only, when no future regrowth matters, I land everything remaining that I legally can.

- The general rule: in any shared, regrowing commons with a trigger-happy enforcer, the winning move is strict sustainability every round. My final score was ruined by matching the defectors instead of being the one boat that kept the ground alive.
